tldr: Instead of forcing heterogeneous robots into a unified action space, DyPES-VLA shares physics understanding ("dynamics priors") across all embodiments and assigns embodiment-specific control to dedicated experts via an MoE action head. Using a single checkpoint across simulation and real-world robots (single-arm, dual-arm, humanoid), it significantly outperforms prior models in manipulation.
hero_caption: Overview of the DyPES-VLA training paradigm. Learning shared dynamics priors from diverse robot data (single-arm, dual-arm, humanoid) via a future-prediction head, and routing robot-specific control through an MoE action head, achieves strong transfer performance without manually forcing action spaces into a single format.
overview:
To build generalist manipulation policies capable of operating across diverse robots, training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models on cross-embodiment data has become a popular approach. However, existing methods face two major hurdles. First, training solely on action-prediction labels fails to fully leverage the rich physical dynamics—such as object motion and contact—found in large collections of human and robot video data. Second, they rely on extensive manual preprocessing (e.g., coordinate transforms or inverse kinematics) to force heterogeneous action spaces with distinct kinematics and control frequencies into a common format. This entangles robot-specific kinematic constraints with shared physical knowledge.

To address this, the authors introduce DyPES-VLA, which architecturally decouples the physics knowledge shared across all robots from embodiment-specific control. Specifically, they apply a future-prediction objective to shared query representations, embedding dynamics priors of object motion and contact changes even from action-free videos. For action generation, they employ a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) action head where temporal attention layers are shared across robots, while embodiment-specific feed-forward network (FFN) experts handle execution directly in each robot's native action space via static routing.

In evaluations across three structurally distinct simulation benchmarks—single-arm (LIBERO), dual-arm (RoboTwin 2.0), and humanoid (RoboCasa-GR1)—a single checkpoint achieved state-of-the-art results across all three. Furthermore, on real hardware using a single model across a single-arm (FR3), dual-arm (COBOT Magic), and humanoid (Unitree G1), DyPES-VLA reached an impressive 75.6% success rate, significantly outperforming prior baselines.
contributions: Proposed a new cross-embodiment learning paradigm that clearly separates shared dynamics priors from embodiment-specific control.

Introduced a query interface that learns object motion and contact transitions from action-free videos via future prediction, while detaching the future generation head at inference time for fast execution.
Introduced an MoE action head operating directly in each robot's native action space, eliminating the need for manual action space alignment.

Demonstrated state-of-the-art generalist manipulation performance with a single checkpoint across three simulation benchmarks and three real-world platforms spanning single-arm, dual-arm, and humanoid robots.

sections.heading: Different Bodies, Same Physical Laws
sections.summary: This section outlines the challenges of adapting a single VLA model to diverse robot embodiments and presents the core design philosophy of DyPES-VLA. To overcome the limitations of manual action unification and action-only supervision, it combines shared physics acquisition via future prediction with embodiment-specific control via MoE.
sections.details:
While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved remarkable progress, most remain tied to specific robot hardware. When building a generalist policy across diverse robots, the core question is: what should be shared across all embodiments, and what should be kept embodiment-specific?

The authors highlight two fundamental shortcomings of existing cross-embodiment VLAs:
- Underusing dynamics priors: Relying solely on action labels leaves the rich physical patterns of object movement, contact, and environmental transitions found in abundant human and robot videos largely untapped.
- Forcing action spaces into a common format: Manually mapping to end-effector poses or using inverse kinematics does not scale across embodiments. It inadvertently entangles shared physical interactions with embodiment-specific control semantics.

To solve these problems, the authors propose DyPES-VLA. This study targets three distinct robot categories with differing degrees of freedom and morphologies: single-arm (Franka Panda / FR3), dual-arm (ALOHA-AgileX / COBOT Magic), and humanoid (Fourier GR-1 / Unitree G1). By training latent VLM queries with a future-prediction objective, the model captures shared physical dynamics. These queries are then passed to an MoE action head to directly decode into each robot's native action space, seamlessly fusing cross-embodiment knowledge without manual pre-alignment.

captions.F1: The learning concept of DyPES-VLA. From heterogeneous robot data (top), the VLM and future-prediction head capture shared physical priors, which the MoE action head (bottom) translates into embodiment-specific control commands.

sections.heading: Cross-Embodiment Learning and the Lineage of Future-Prediction Models
sections.summary: This section reviews the evolution of VLA research from embodiment-specific policies to generalists, categorizing existing cross-embodiment approaches. It also contrasts DyPES-VLA with world-model-based future-prediction methods to clarify its positioning.
sections.details:
Cross-embodiment VLA methods can be broadly categorized into three approaches based on where they handle embodiment-specific differences:

- Common action space mapping: Designing manual end-effector frames or mapping into latent spaces. However, these obscure robot-specific kinematic limits and blend them with shared physical understanding.
- Prompting and conditioning: Using robot IDs or soft prompts to condition a single shared network. These often struggle to handle fundamental differences in degrees of freedom and kinematics.
- Architectural modular separation: Dedicating separate input or output heads to each robot. DyPES-VLA advances this line by placing the shared interface upstream—at the query state trained via future prediction—and routing it to downstream expert modules.

Meanwhile, learning via future prediction (such as World-Action Models or UWM) has gained traction, but generating future images alongside actions during inference imposes heavy computational overhead, creating a bottleneck for real-time control. DyPES-VLA crucially differs: it uses future prediction strictly as a regularizer during pre-training to shape shared physics representations, and fully detaches the future generation head at inference time.

sections.heading: Learning Physics via Future Prediction, Executing Control via Experts
sections.summary: This section explains the building blocks and two-stage training pipeline of DyPES-VLA. It generates shared queries via a VLM, learns physical dynamics with a SANA-based future-prediction head, and outputs native actions using a Diffusion Transformer-based MoE head.
sections.details:
As shown in Figure F2, the overall DyPES-VLA architecture consists of three components: a shared query interface, a future generation head, and an MoE action head.

3.1 & 3.2 Shared Query Interface
Visual images, natural language instructions, and robot metadata $m_e$ (robot type, control frequency, camera setup, etc.) are fed into the VLM (Qwen3-VL-2B). Appending $N=96$ learnable query tokens to this sequence allows extracting the query state $\mathbf{Z}$ from the final hidden layer. This $\mathbf{Z}$ serves as the shared interface connecting future prediction and action generation.

3.3 Learning Shared Dynamics Priors
The future generation head adopts the SANA-600M image generation model. It predicts the future frame offset by a time horizon $\Delta_e$ (corresponding to each robot's action chunk length) from the current observation. Crucially, the current image is not fed directly into this head; only the query state $\mathbf{Z}$ is provided via cross-attention. This forces $\mathbf{Z}$ to compress all object motions and contact transitions necessary to predict the future.

3.4 Embodiment-Specific MoE Action Head
Action generation is handled by a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) based on Flow Matching. Lightweight embodiment-specific encoders and decoders convert between input actions and output velocities. Inside the DiT, temporal self-attention and cross-attention over the query $\mathbf{Z}$ are shared across all robots, while subsequent feed-forward network (FFN) layers statically route tokens to dedicated experts based on robot metadata. This allows the model to share temporal motion structures while absorbing individual kinematic constraints within dedicated FFNs.

3.5 Two-Stage Training Pipeline
- Stage 1 (Pre-training): The VLM and future generation head are trained solely on future-prediction loss using action-free human manipulation videos (EgoDex) and simulation data.
- Stage 2 (Joint Training): The future-prediction loss and action-generation loss are jointly optimized using multi-robot data with action labels. At inference time, the future generation head is discarded, incurring zero extra runtime cost.

captions.F2: The overall architecture and training pipeline of DyPES-VLA. (a) The VLM extracts a shared query state from observations and instructions, passing it to the future generation head and the MoE action head. (b) The two-stage training scheme: Stage 1 learns physics from action-free videos, and Stage 2 performs joint training with multi-robot data.

sections.heading: Dominating Single-Arm, Dual-Arm, and Humanoid in Simulation, and 75.6% on Real Hardware
sections.summary: This section evaluates DyPES-VLA across three simulation benchmarks and three real robot platforms. A single checkpoint outperforms benchmark-specific SOTA models and substantially leads baselines in real-world trials. Ablations and linear probe analyses confirm that future prediction directly improves contact prediction capabilities.
sections.details:
The experiments rigorously examine how well DyPES-VLA generalizes across heterogeneous robot environments.

4.1 & 4.2 Simulation Results (Q1)
Using a single checkpoint without task-specific fine-tuning, the model was evaluated across three representative benchmarks:
- RoboTwin 2.0 (14-DoF dual-arm): Achieved 88.78% in the canonical setting, 89.26% under randomized background and lighting, averaging 89.02%—surpassing the generalist competitor Qwen-VLA (86.65%) by 2.37 points.
- RoboCasa-GR1 (29-DoF humanoid): Reached a 59.25% success rate, outperforming the benchmark-specific SOTA ABot-M0 (58.3%) and the world-model-based LDA-1B (55.4%).
- LIBERO (7-DoF single-arm): Achieved 98.0%, setting top-tier performance over Fast-WAM (97.6%) and others.

4.3 Real-World Robot Evaluation (Q1)
Starting from the simulation-pretrained weights, the policy was jointly fine-tuned on three physical platforms (7-DoF single-arm FR3, 14-DoF dual-arm COBOT Magic, humanoid Unitree G1) across three tasks: kiwi storage, water pouring, and bookshelf placement. While independently trained ACT averaged 32.4% and the strong generalist GR00T-N1.6 reached 59.6%, DyPES-VLA achieved an outstanding 75.6% average success rate.

4.4 Ablation Studies (Q2, Q3, Q4)
Removing the future-prediction loss caused a drop of 2.4 points on RoboTwin 2.0 and 2.5 points on RoboCasa-GR1. Replacing the MoE with a single dense FFN degraded performance by up to 2.1 points, and removing metadata context also harmed results.

4.5 Latent Representation Probing (Q2)
To confirm whether future prediction truly captures physical dynamics, linear probes were trained on frozen query states $\mathbf{Z}$ to detect future contact onset and release. The model trained with future prediction showed substantial gains in AUROC and AUPRC over the variant without it, demonstrating that contact dynamics are encoded in a linearly separable form within the queries.

captions.F3: Rollout frames of the kiwi storage task across three real-world platforms (top: FR3 single-arm, middle: COBOT Magic dual-arm, bottom: Unitree G1 humanoid). A single fine-tuned checkpoint directly produces smooth motions tailored to each robot's degrees of freedom and morphology.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Diverse Embodiments, Shared Physics, Dedicated Control
sections.summary: This section summarizes the findings. Combining shared dynamics prior learning with embodiment-specific MoE control makes DyPES-VLA an effective unified foundation for manipulation across single-arm, dual-arm, and humanoid robots.
sections.details:
This work introduces a new paradigm for sharing manipulation knowledge across diverse robot morphologies and instantiates it as DyPES-VLA.

The strength of this approach lies in learning physical rules—such as object motion and contact—from action-free videos via future prediction, and translating them into robot-specific controls through an MoE structure without forced action alignment. Across single-arm, dual-arm, and humanoid robots, it outperformed both specialized and generalist baselines in simulation and on real hardware. Requiring no manual alignment, this approach offers a promising path toward scaling to even more robot types and real-world environments.

sections.heading: Appendix: Benchmark Details and Qualitative Real-World Rollouts
sections.summary: This section presents detailed success rates across all 24 tasks in RoboCasa-GR1 and 50 tasks in RoboTwin 2.0, alongside qualitative rollout sequences for water pouring and bookshelf placement on real hardware.
sections.details:
The appendix provides comprehensive experimental results and real-world rollouts omitted from the main text.

- RoboCasa-GR1 Breakdown: Across all 24 tasks (1,200 total trials), it maintains steady performance regardless of difficulty, achieving 55.3% on movable storage tasks and 60.6% on container transfer tasks.
- RoboTwin 2.0 Breakdown: Across all 50 tasks, it averages 88.78% in canonical conditions and 89.26% under perturbed lighting and layouts, demonstrating strong robustness against visual and spatial disturbances.
- Additional Real-World Tasks: For pouring water into a bowl (Figure F4) and placing a book on a shelf (Figure F5), each platform (single-arm, dual-arm, humanoid) effectively uses its respective arm degrees of freedom to successfully complete the tasks.

captions.F4: Water pouring task rollouts on three real-world robots (FR3, COBOT Magic, G1). Each robot accurately handles delicate contact and trajectory adjustments, such as spout alignment and tilting angle control.

takeaways: In cross-embodiment learning, sharing physical dynamics globally while distributing action generation across robot-specific MoE FFNs is far more effective than forcing actions into a single shared space.
Using a future-prediction objective to regularize latent query representations allows policies to efficiently absorb contact and motion priors from action-free videos (such as human demonstrations).
Detaching the future-image generation head during inference enables the policy to maintain fast control frequencies without the heavy computational burden of world models.
A single checkpoint co-trained across heterogeneous simulation environments serves as a powerful pre-trained foundation for transfer to real-world single-arm, dual-arm, and humanoid robots.
limitations: Because routing relies on static metadata-based selection, zero-shot transfer to an entirely unseen robot kinematic configuration is not directly supported, requiring a new expert module to be trained.
The policy relies purely on visual observations without proprioceptive inputs (such as current joint angles), which may limit precise positioning under camera blind spots or severe occlusion.

The pre-training future-prediction target is based on a single viewpoint from the primary camera, meaning 3D geometric consistency across multi-camera setups might not be explicitly learned as part of the dynamics.
